title: Potatoes Grow in Moon Dust
summary: If people are going to live on the Moon, they will need to eat. And shipping every meal from Earth would cost a fortune. So scientists are testing whether astronauts could grow their own food in lunar soil. A team from Oregon State University has now grown potatoes in simulated moon dust, and the spuds completed their entire life cycle. The researchers published their findings on November 20 in the journal Microgravity. The Moon's surface is covered in regolith, a layer of dust and broken rock. It is not like soil on Earth: it has no nutrients and contains compounds that can harm plants. To test it, the team used five different materials that mimic regolith from the Moon's flat plains, called maria, and its highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a nutrient-rich soil made with the help of worms. The team mixed different amounts of it into the fake regolith. They found that regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as regular soil for growing potatoes. 'We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,' said Aymeric Goyer, an associate professor at Oregon State. 'That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon.' The compost seems to help in two ways: it adds nutrients, and it may shield the plants from some of the harmful compounds in lunar dust. 'We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds,' said David Handy, a researcher in Goyer's lab. The idea is that future astronauts could carry a small amount of nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with the dust already on the Moon. NASA, which plans to build a permanent base on the Moon, helped fund the research. Potatoes are a good first crop to test: they are filling, they grow underground, and they can be cooked in many ways. If they can thrive in moon dust, a lunar vegetable garden may not be far behind.
why_it_matters: If astronauts can grow food on the Moon, future moon bases could feed themselves instead of depending on costly shipments from Earth.

background_read: The Moon's surface is covered in regolith, a layer of dust and broken rock with no nutrients for plants, so nothing can grow in it as it is.
Plants need nutrients from soil to grow, and compost made from decaying matter adds those nutrients and can also shield roots from harmful substances.
NASA plans to build a permanent base on the Moon, and astronauts living there would need a steady supply of fresh food, which is hard to ship from Earth.
